sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Single Arm Dumbbell Shrug is a unilateral trapezius exercise performed with a dumbbell in one hand while standing.

By loading one side at a time, this variation allows for greater range of motion, identifies and corrects muscular imbalances between sides, and improves mind-muscle connection with the trap.

This is an excellent accessory movement for balanced upper back development.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Corrects left-right muscular imbalances
- Greater range of motion per side
- Improved mind-muscle connection
- Core and obliques engage for stabilization
- Reduced total spinal load compared to bilateral versions
- Convenient — only one dumbbell required
- Great accessory for heavier bilateral shrug work

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Upper Trapezius

Secondary: Levator Scapulae, Rhomboids, Obliques, Core Stabilizers, Forearms and Grip

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart.
2. Select a dumbbell of appropriate weight.
3. Hold the dumbbell in one hand by your side with a neutral grip.
4. Let the free arm hang relaxed or rest on your hip.
5. Keep your back straight and chest lifted.
6. Engage your core for stability.
7. Keep shoulders relaxed and down to start.

sections.heading: Execution
sections.content:
1. Lift your shoulder on the side with the dumbbell as high as possible by shrugging it towards your ear.
2. Keep the arm straight throughout the movement.
3. Squeeze the trapezius at the top of the movement.
4. Lower your shoulder back down under control.
5. Repeat the shrug for the desired number of repetitions.
6. Focus on engaging your shoulder muscles.
7. Maintain proper form throughout the movement.
8. Switch to the other arm and repeat for balanced training.
9. Adjust the weight as needed.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Leaning sideways to assist the lift
- Bending the arm during the shrug
- Rolling the shoulder instead of shrugging straight up
- Using too much weight and losing form
- Insufficient range of motion
- Rushing the reps without control
- Not pausing at the top
- Training one side significantly heavier than the other

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Single Dumbbell
- Optional: Lifting Strap (for grip assistance)
- Optional: Chalk (improves grip)
- Flat-soled shoes recommended

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Stance: Feet shoulder-width apart.
2. Grip: Neutral grip on the dumbbell.
3. Working Arm: Fully extended at your side.
4. Free Arm: Relaxed at your side or on your hip.
5. Chest: Lifted, shoulders back.
6. Back: Straight with natural arch.
7. Head: Neutral, eyes forward.
8. Core: Engaged to prevent side lean.

sections.heading: Progression Tips
sections.content:
1. Start with a light dumbbell to learn the movement.
2. Focus on straight-up shrug motion.
3. Use the mirror to check for side-lean.
4. Pause at the top for peak contraction.
5. Start with the weaker side to ensure balanced volume.
6. Gradually increase weight as strength improves.
7. Use a strap when grip becomes limiting.
8. Keep reps in the 10-15 range for hypertrophy.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Dumbbell Shrug: Bilateral standing variation
- Seated Dumbbell Shrug: Removes lower body involvement
- Barbell Shrug: Heaviest loading option
- Smith Machine Shrug: Fixed bar path
- Cable Shrug: Constant tension variation
- Kettlebell Shrug: Alternative implement

sections.heading: Trap Variations
sections.content:
Dumbbell Shrug: Classic bilateral variation
Seated Dumbbell Shrug: Seated isolation
Barbell Shrug: Heavy trap builder
Trap Bar Shrug: Neutral hand position
Smith Machine Shrug: Fixed path version
Farmer's Carry: Dynamic trap and grip work

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Shoulder Impingement: Neutral grip is usually shoulder-friendly
Grip Issues: Use a lifting strap
Lower Back Pain: Engage the core firmly to prevent side-lean
Limited Mobility: Reduce range of motion
Muscle Imbalance: Start with and match reps to the weaker side
Beginner: Start light to master balance and form
